author: श्रीमदानन्दतीर्थभगवत्पादाचार्य
commentary:
ज्ञानफलमाह - बुद्धियुक्त इति ॥ सुकृतमप्यप्रियं मानुष्यादिफलं जहाति, न बृहत्फलमपि उपासनादिनिमित्तम् । ‘न हास्य (न तस्य)कर्म क्षीयते’, ‘अविदित्वाऽस्मिन् लोके जुहोति यजते तपस्तप्यते बहूनि वर्षसहस्राणि अन्तवदेवास्य तद् भवति’ इत्यादिश्रुतिस्मृतिभ्यः । अतः कर्मक्षयश्रुतिरज्ञानिविषया सर्वत्र । उभयक्षयश्रुतिरप्यनिष्टविषया । नहीष्टपुण्यक्षये किञ्चित् प्रयोजनम् । न चेष्टनाशो ज्ञानिनो युक्तः । इष्टाश्च केचिद्विषयाः - ‘स यदि पितृलोककामो भवति सङ्कल्पादेवास्य पितरः समुत्तिष्ठन्ति’, ‘प्रजापतेः सभां वेश्म प्रपद्ये । यशोऽहं भवामि ब्राह्मणानाम्’, ‘स्त्रीभिर्वा यानैर्वा’, ‘अस्माद्ध्येवात्मनो यद्यत् कामयते तत्तत् सृजते’, ‘कामान्नी कामरूप्यनुसञ्जरन्’, ‘स एकधा भवति’ इत्यादिश्रुतिभ्यः । बहुत्वेऽप्यात्मसुखस्य पुनरिष्टत्वात् कर्मसुखे न विरोधः । अनुभवशक्तिश्चेश्वरप्रसादात् । श्रुतेश्च । न च शरीरपातात् पूर्वमेतत् - ‘स तत्र पर्येति’, ‘एतमानन्दमयमात्मानमुपसङ्क्रम्य’ इत्याद्युत्तरत्र श्रवणात् । 

न चैकीभूत एव ब्रह्मणा सः । ‘मग्नस्य हि परेऽज्ञाने किं नु दुःखतरं भवेत्’ इत्यादिनिन्दनाद् मोक्षधर्मे । परिहारे पृथग् भोगाभिधानाच्च । शुकादीनां पृथग्दृष्टेश्च । ‘जगद्व्यापारवर्जम्’ इत्यैश्वर्यमर्यादोक्तेश्च । ‘इदं ज्ञानमु(म)पाश्रित्य मम साधर्म्यमागताः’ इति च । उपाधिनाशे नाशाच्च प्रतिबिम्बस्य । न चैकीभूतस्य पृथग्ज्ञाने मानं पश्यामः । ‘आसं दुःखी, नाऽसम्’ इति ज्ञानविरोधाच्चेश्वरस्य । अनेन रूपेणेति च । भेदाभावात् । 

न च प्रतिबिम्बस्य बिम्बैक्यं लोके पश्यामः । उपाधिनाशे मानं वा । ‘मग्नस्य हि परेऽज्ञाने’ इति दुःखात्मकत्वोक्तेश्च । ‘यावदात्मभावित्वाद्’ इत्युपाधिनित्यताभिधानाच्च। अतोऽन्यवचनं प्रतीयमानमप्यौपचारिकम् । दृष्टाश्च ते भगवतो भिन्ना नारदेन । प्रतिशाखं च ‘स एकधा’ इत्यादिषु भेदेन प्रतीयन्ते । विरोधे तु युक्तिमतामेव बलवत्त्वम् । युक्तयश्चात्रोक्ताः - ‘मग्नस्य हि’ इत्यादयः। अतो जले जलैकीभाववत् एकीभावः । उक्तं च - ‘यथोदकं शुद्धे शुद्धम्’, ‘यथा नद्यः’ इत्यादौ । तत्राऽप्यन्योन्यात्मकत्वे वृद्ध्यसम्भवः । अस्ति चेषत् समुद्रेऽपि द्वारि । महत्त्वाद् अन्यत्रादृष्टिः । 

‘ता एवापो ददौ तस्य स ऋषिः शंसितव्रतः’ इति महाकौर्मे समर्थानां भेदज्ञानाच्च । 

‘नैव तत् प्राप्नुवन्त्येते ब्रह्मेशानादयः सुराः । यत् ते पदं हि कैवल्यम्’ इति निषेधाच्च, नारदीये । सविचारश्च निर्णयः कृतो मोक्षधर्मेषु । बलवांश्च सविचारो निर्णयो वाक्यमात्रात् । अतो ‘यत्र नान्यत् पश्यति’ इत्याद्यपि तदधीनसत्तादिवाचि । अन्यथा कथम् ऐश्वर्यादि स्यात्? न च तन्मायामयम् इत्युक्तम् । अन्यथा कथं तत्रैव ‘स एकधा’ इत्यादि ब्रूयात् । न च –‘न ह वै सशरीरस्य’ इत्यादिविरोधः । वैलक्षण्यात् तच्छरीराणाम् । अभौतिकानि हि तानि नित्योपाधिविनिर्मितानीश्वरशक्त्या । तथाचोक्तम्– ‘शरीरं जायते तेषां षोडश्या कलयैव तु’ इत्यादि नारायणाष्टाक्षरकल्पे । वदन्ति च लौकिकवैलक्षण्येऽभावशब्दम्- ‘अप्रहर्षमनानन्दम्’, ‘सुखदुःखबाह्यः’ इत्यादिषु । निरुक्त्यभावाच्च न तानि शरीराणि । तथा हि श्रुतिः - ‘अशारीतीँ.... तच्छरीरमभवद्’ इति । न हि तानि शीर्णानि भवन्ति । ‘सर्गेऽपि नोपजायन्ते’ इत्यादिवचनात् । साम्यात् प्रयोगः । प्रयोगाच्च - ‘अनिन्द्रिया अनाहारा अनिष्पन्दाः सुगन्धिनः’, ‘देहेन्द्रियासुहीनानां वैकुण्ठपुरवासिनाम्’ इत्यादि दृष्टदेहेष्वेव । न चैषाऽन्या गौणी मुक्तिः । 

‘बहुनाऽत्र किमुक्तेन यावच्छ्वेतं न गच्छति । योगी तावन्न मुक्तः स्याद् एष शास्त्रस्य निर्णयः ॥’ इत्यादित्यपुराणे तदन्यमुक्तिनिषेधात् । ये त्वत्रैव भगवन्तं प्रविशन्ति तेऽपि पश्चात् तत्रैव यान्ति । योग्यत्वं चात्र विवक्षितम् । युधिष्ठिरप्रश्न इतरनिन्दनाच्च । सायुज्यं च ग्रहवत् । तदुक्तेश्च - ‘भुञ्जते पुरुषं प्राप्य यथा देवग्रहादयः । तथा मुक्तावुत्तमायां बाह्यान् भोगांस्तु भुञ्जते ॥’ इति नारायणाष्टाक्षरकल्पे । अतोऽनिष्टस्यैव वियोगः । सोऽस्त्येव सर्वात्मना– ‘अदुःखम्’, ‘सर्वदुःखविवर्जिताः’, ‘अशोकमहिमम्’, ‘यत्र गत्वा न शोचति’ इत्यादिभ्यः । विशेषवचनाभावाच्च । येषां त्वीषद् दृश्यते ते न सायुज्यं प्राप्ताः । सामीप्याद्येव तेषाम् । अतः प्रारब्धकर्मशेषभावात् तद् भुक्त्वा सायुज्यं गच्छन्ति । तच्चोक्तम्- 

‘सङ्कर्षणादयः सर्वे स्वाधिकाराद् अनन्तरम् । प्रविशन्ति परं देवं विष्णुं नास्त्यत्र संशयः ॥’ इति व्यासयोगे । अतोऽनिष्टस्य सर्वात्मना वियोगः । ‘परब्रह्मत्वमिच्छामि परमात्मन् (परब्रह्मन्)जनार्दन’ । इत्यादिना ब्रह्मादिभिरपि प्रार्थितत्वात् । ‘न मोक्षसदृशं किञ्चिद् अधिकं वा सुखं क्वचित् । ऋते वैष्णवमानन्दं वाङ्मनोगोचरं महत् ॥’ इत्यादेश्च ब्रह्मादिपदादपि अधिकतमं सुखं च मोक्ष इति सिद्धम् । अतो योगाय युज्यस्व । ज्ञानोपायाय । तद्धि कर्मकौशलम् ॥ ५० ॥
translation:
Krishna states the fruit of spiritual knowledge by using the words beginning with “Buddhi-yuktaḥ” (one endowed with spiritual intelligence). Such a person casts away even Sukritam (pious material actions) which lead to undesirable outcomes like human rebirth and similar fruits; but he does not lose the great fruits (Brihat-phalam) born out of Upasana (spiritual worship and meditation) and similar causes. This is confirmed by Vedic scriptures (Shruti) and traditional histories (Smriti) which state: “For him, spiritual actions are never exhausted,” and “Without knowing Him, if one performs sacrifices, offers oblations, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years, all of that fruit remains purely temporary and finite.” Therefore, scriptural statements regarding the absolute exhaustion or destruction of all actions (Karma-kshaya) apply everywhere specifically to the ignorant people (Ajnani). The scriptural statements concerning the destruction of 'both types of actions' (pious and impious) actually refer specifically to the destruction of undesirable actions (Anishta). For there is absolutely no benefit or purpose in destroying desirable, spiritually pure merit (Ishta-punya). Moreover, the destruction of desirable spiritual assets is not logical or fitting for an enlightened soul (Jnani). And certain desired spiritual objects and experiences indeed exist in liberation, as proven by various Vedic passages: “If he desires the world of the ancestors, by his mere wish/will, the ancestors rise up,” “I attain the assembly hall and abode of Prajapati; I become glorious among the knowers of Brahman,” “Moving about with spiritual women or spiritual vehicles,” “Whatever he desires from this Supreme Soul, all that is created,” “Consuming foods according to his desire, assuming forms according to his desire, moving about freely,” and “He manifests in one form [or multiple forms]. Even though there is multiplicity and abundance of the soul's innate bliss (Atma-sukha), because it is highly desired, there is no contradiction with the enjoyment of the fruits of spiritualized actions. And the capacity to experience this bliss is granted solely by the grace of the Supreme Lord (Ishvara-prasada). This is also supported by the Vedas. And this state does not happen prior to the falling of the physical body; because later scriptural passages state: “He moves around there [in the spiritual realm],” and “Having approached this Supreme Soul who is filled with bliss.” 

Furthermore, that liberated soul does not become completely identical or merged as one substance with Brahman. Because of the strong condemnation found in the Moksha Dharma sections of the Mahabharata: “For one who is submerged in total ignorance/unconsciousness of the Supreme, what can be more deeply painful than that? And because in the descriptions of final liberation, individual, distinct enjoyment (Prithag-bhoga) is explicitly declared. And because perfect sages like Shuka Deva and others are seen to maintain distinct, individual perceptions. And because the boundary and limit of the soul's spiritual power is explicitly defined in the Brahma Sutras as: “Except for the cosmic function of universal creation, maintenance, and destruction (Jagad-vyāpāra-varjam).” And because Krishna states later (BG 14.2): “Taking shelter of this knowledge, they attain a nature similar to Mine (Mama sādharmyam-āgatāḥ).” For if the conditioning medium (Upadhi) is destroyed, the reflection (Pratibimba, the soul) would be completely destroyed. And we see absolutely no valid scriptural evidence (Manam) for an individual who has become identical with Brahman to possess distinct, separate awareness. Moreover, this would contradict the eternal omniscience of God, who would have to possess the conflicting knowledge: “I was once miserable [when I was a bound soul], and now I am not.” By the phrase “with this form,” it implies distinction; otherwise, there would be an absence of any difference. We never observe in common worldly experience any actual identity between a reflection and the original object (Bimba). Nor is there valid proof for the total destruction of the soul's essential, spiritual medium. And because, as quoted before, “being submerged in total ignorance” is explicitly described as a state of suffering. And because the eternal nature of the soul's spiritual body/medium is declared in the Brahma Sutras: “Because it co-exists as long as the soul itself exists (Yāvad-ātma-bhāvitvāt).” 

Therefore, any scriptural statements that appear to say otherwise are merely metaphorical or figurative (Aupacharikam). And those liberated souls were directly seen as distinct from the Supreme Lord by the great sage Narada. And across every branch of the Vedas, in passages like “He is of one form [then manifests as many],” they are understood to exist in a state of distinct difference. Whenever there is an apparent scriptural contradiction, those statements that are supported by sound, flawless logic (Yukti) possess greater strength and weight. And the logical arguments have already been stated here, such as the verse “For one who is submerged in total ignorance...” and others. Therefore, the 'becoming one' (Eki-bhava) spoken of in scripture is exactly like the mixing of water with water. And it has been stated in the Katha Upanishad and Mundaka Upanishad: “As pure water poured into pure water [remains distinct but similar],” and “As rivers [enter the ocean]...” Even in those examples, if they became absolutely identical in substance, an increase in volume (when a river enters the ocean) would be impossible. And a slight, distinct difference can still be perceived at the mouth where the river meets the ocean. Due to the immense, vast scale of the ocean everywhere else, the subtle difference is simply not visible to ordinary eyes. And because highly capable, spiritually powerful beings retain the knowledge of distinction, as stated in the Maha-Kurma Purana: “That sage of strict vows gave back those very same distinct drops of water to him.” And because there is an explicit prohibition in the Naradiya Purana: “Even cosmic demigods like Brahma, Shiva, and others can never equal or fully possess that supreme status of absolute purity (Kaivalyam) which is Your exclusive domain.” And a highly reasoned, analytical conclusion has been established in the Moksha Dharma sections. A reasoned, thoroughly investigated conclusion is always far more powerful than a mere literal isolated sentence.

Therefore, Vedic passages like “Where one sees no other...” (Chandogya Upanishad) actually express that everything else has an existence entirely dependent upon and subordinate to Him (Tad-adhina-satta). Otherwise, if there were absolute non-existence of everything else, how could the extraordinary spiritual opulence and power (Aishwarya) of the liberated soul exist? And it has already been stated that this opulence is not an illusion or made of material Maya. Otherwise, how could that very same scriptural text say, “He exists in one form, [then three forms, then five forms]”? Nor is there any contradiction with Vedic statements like, “Verily, for one who has a body, there is no escape from pleasure and pain.” Because the spiritual bodies of the liberated souls possess a completely different, extraordinary nature (Vailakshanya). For those bodies are completely non-material (Abhautika), constructed out of an eternal spiritual medium by the divine power of the Supreme Lord (Ishvara-shaktya). And thus it is stated in the Narayana-Ashtakshara-Kalpa: “Their spiritual body manifests purely from the sixteenth transcendental portion [untainted by material nature].” Scriptures use words indicating 'absence' or 'negation' simply to denote a complete departure from worldly, material characteristics, as seen in expressions like: “Without worldly excitement, without material pleasure,” and “Far outside the realm of material happiness and suffering.” And by technical etymological definition, those are not standard physical bodies (which decay). For the Vedic text states: “He became un-embodied... that became his non-decaying spiritual form.” For those spiritual forms never shrivel, rot, or shatter (Sheernani). This is supported by Krishna’s own statement later (BG 14.2): “Even at the time of universal creation, they are not born.” The word 'body' is used there only due to a loose similarity in appearance and function. And because scriptural descriptions such as: “Without material senses, without consuming material food, without material breath, yet beautifully fragrant,” and “The residents of the spiritual city of Vaikuntha are entirely devoid of gross material bodies, physical senses, and vital material breaths,” apply exclusively to contrast them with seen, worldly bodies. 

And one should not claim that this individual spiritual existence is a secondary, lower, or figurative type of liberation (Gauni Mukti). Because any other type of liberation is explicitly rejected in the Aditya Purana: “What is the use of speaking at length? As long as a practitioner does not reach the white, luminous spiritual realm (Shveta-dvipa), that yogi is not considered truly liberated. This is the final, unshakeable conclusion of the sacred scriptures.” Those who appear to enter into the body of the Supreme Lord right here on earth, they also subsequently go to that very same spiritual realm. And it is the distinct, innate spiritual fitness and qualification (Yogyatvam) of the soul that is intended to be described here. This is also clear from the questions asked by Yudhishthira and the explicit criticism of alternative, imperfect ideas. The state of intimate, merged communion (Sayujya) is to be understood like a celestial body possessing or overshadowing a medium. As it is declared in the Narayana-Ashtakshara-Kalpa: “Just as powerful celestial deities enter into and experience through a medium, exactly so, having attained the Supreme Being (Purusha), the souls in the highest state of liberation experience and enjoy external, transcendent pleasures.” Therefore, liberation means exclusively the separation (Viyoga) from that which is undesirable and painful (Anishta). And that total separation from suffering absolutely exists in its entirety, as declared in passages: “Devoid of pain,” “Completely freed from all miseries,” “Established in a glorious state free of grief,” and “Going where one never laments.” And because there are no scriptural statements indicating any specific destruction of the soul's positive, blissful qualities. For those souls in whom a tiny trace of material connection or perception is still seen, they have not yet entered the absolute state of Sayujya; they possess stages like Samipya (proximity to God) and others. Therefore, due to the remaining presence of a trace of Prarabdha Karma, after experiencing and exhausting that remnant, they confidently enter into total Sayujya liberation. And this has been explicitly stated in the Vyasa Yoga: “Great cosmic divinities like Sankarshana and others, immediately after completing their universal duties (Sva-adhikarat), enter into the Supreme Lord Vishnu; there is absolutely no doubt regarding this.” Therefore, liberation is firmly defined as the complete, absolute separation from everything that is undesirable. Because this very state is prayed for even by cosmic creators like Brahma and others, who say: “O Supreme Soul! O Janardana! I desire to be fully situated in the nature of Brahman.” And from statements such as: “There is no happiness anywhere that is equal to or greater than liberation—which is the grand, immense bliss of Vishnu (Vaishnava-ananda) lying far beyond the reach of ordinary speech and mind,” it is absolutely established (Siddham) that liberation is a state of happiness that vastly exceeds even the highest cosmic positions like that of Brahma. Therefore, prepare yourself and strive for this Yoga! Strive for this practical method characterized by spiritual knowledge. For that method alone constitutes true cleverness, skill, and expertise in action (Karma-kaushalam).
